case_studies.title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
case_studies.abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.
case_studies.summary: Cap-and-Track lets you adapt LLM inference dispatch to changing GPU capacity and request size without hard‑coding a rate. They built an async dispatcher that rejects requests early when resources are full, then uses those refusals to probe capacity and refill queues, cutting GPU use by 43% in production. It’s relevant to anyone managing AI inference fleets, offering a way to save hardware while keeping high‑priority work on time.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage GPU fleets for LLM inference, use Cap-and-Track by: 1) Add a fail‑fast admission check that rejects over‑capacity requests; 2) Log refusals and use them to back‑off and probe current capacity; 3) Keep short‑lived queues in the inference engine to batch efficiently. This will reduce GPU usage and improve throughput without manual retuning.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a practical system for dispatching LLM inference requests that directly addresses resource allocation in large-scale AI deployments, which is highly relevant for infrastructure engineers managing cloud-based LLM services. The authors mention a live implementation at Meta, indicating the system is built and tested. While the technique could be adopted to reduce cost and improve throughput for enterprises, it is not a turnkey product but a methodology that can be implemented within the next month by experienced engineers. Thus all three criteria score in the high‑to‑mid range, yielding a strong total score.

case_studies.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
case_studies.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
case_studies.summary: GateWatch offers a very lightweight way to watch what large language models (LLMs) do by turning a few key features into simple Boolean rules. They built a system that keeps memory use down by 99.98% and adds almost no lag when running many probes on a model like Gemma‑2‑9B. The result is accurate monitoring that almost matches heavier methods while staying fast and tiny.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM deployments, add GateWatch to your monitoring stack: 1) Identify the key SAE features you need (about 4), 2) Deploy GateWatchServe to stream these binaries during inference, 3) Use the compact lookup tables to evaluate probes in parallel, keeping throughput above 97% and cache usage near 100%.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical monitoring tool for LLMs, directly impacting deployment, debugging, and compliance for infrastructure teams. It includes a released prototype (GateWatchServe) integrated with vLLM, indicating real-world readiness. While it offers immediate operational benefits, commercialization or service integration would require additional tooling, so monetisation potential is moderate.

case_studies.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.
case_studies.summary: PIPETTE tackles prompt injection attacks on LLM agents by creating a purple‑team framework that pushes red‑team attacks to cover many strategies, then trains defenders with those attacks to build robust agents. It built a dictionary‑reward system for wider attack discovery and an on‑policy training pipeline that keeps normal tasks working while blocking injection. The result was agents with almost zero success for static attacks and strong resistance to adaptive attacks without losing performance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑hosted LLM services, use PIPETTE by: 1) integrating its dictionary‑reward red‑team to generate diverse injection scenarios, 2) feeding those scenarios into an on‑policy adversarial training loop for your models, 3) validating that attack success rates drop to near zero while task accuracy stays near baseline.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses prompt injection attacks on LLM agents, a security concern relevant to IT infrastructure that could affect engineers managing LLM services. The approach includes an implementation and evaluation, indicating a usable system, but the work is still research‑grade with limited real‑world deployment evidence. Commercial use would require integration and testing in existing workflows, which could be done within a few months but is not immediately ready as a product.

case_studies.title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
case_studies.abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.
case_studies.summary: CriticNPU is a tool that speeds up designing neural processing units (NPUs) for large‑language‑model inference by using a fast, physics‑based model to guess whether a new hardware setup will be faster before running a slow simulator. It filters out poor candidates early and then refines the design using real simulation data, cutting the number of expensive simulations in half while matching or beating the best latency in most test cases. This directly helps IT engineers who design or optimise custom AI chips or select cloud AI services, giving a faster way to pick the right hardware configuration for specific workloads.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage NPU or AI workload optimisation, here is what to do: 1) Run CriticNPU’s Roofline model with your target architecture parameters to get quick pre‑simulation estimates of compute and memory bottlenecks. 2) Filter out designs that the critic flags as unlikely to beat your current best. 3) Simulate only the promising candidates and let CriticNPU’s post‑simulation analysis suggest the next parameter tweaks to hit the lowest latency for prefill and decode stages.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a specialized tool for exploring NPU configurations for LLM inference. While it offers sample-efficient design-space exploration and provides code, its relevance to everyday IT infrastructure tasks—such as managing Microsoft 365, AWS, Azure, SSO, or endpoint security—is limited. The tool could be useful for organizations investing heavily in custom AI accelerators, but most IT engineers in the target audience are unlikely to deploy or benefit from it within a short timeframe.
